JSON: Name: chronic_analgesic_anxiety_stage_timing Title: Multivariable analysis of cancer stage at diagnosis by duration of pre-existing chronic analgesic use and anxiety/depression using linked primary care and cancer registry data Short Hypothesis: Among patients diagnosed with lung or colon cancer, recent-onset chronic analgesic medication use (<12 months pre-diagnosis) increases the odds of advanced-stage (III–IV) diagnosis compared with no analgesic use. Related Work: Existing studies examine associations between pre-existing comorbidity and cancer diagnostic delays using summary comorbidity indices, binary comorbidity flags, or counts of prescriptions. Prior approaches include population-level descriptive analyses and regression models relating aggregated comorbidity burden to stage or emergency presentation. Limitations of current methods are inconsistent comorbidity definitions and variable look-back windows, failure to separate medication-based markers (e.g., analgesic/opioid prescriptions) from disease codes, limited disaggregation of timing/duration (recent-onset vs persistent), sparse control for consultation frequency or site-specific symptoms, and mixed handling of mental-health conditions due to under-recording and aggregation of anxiety and depression. Few studies test interactions with age or sex, few stratify by drug type (opioid vs non-opioid), and causal direction (reverse causality) is rarely addressed. There is therefore limited evidence on how timing and type of analgesic prescribing and anxiety/depression recordings modify odds of advanced-stage lung or colon cancer. Abstract: Problem: Pre-existing chronic conditions may alter cancer diagnostic pathways, but existing evidence poorly distinguishes timing and duration of these conditions. Approach: Use linked primary care electronic health records and national cancer registry data to model associations between duration-classified chronic analgesic medication use and anxiety/depression and stage at diagnosis for incident lung and colon cancers. Main contribution: Define and test exposure categories (recent-onset: first record <12 months pre-diagnosis; historic: 12–72 months; persistent: both windows) for medication- and consultation-derived morbidities, and quantify adjusted associations with advanced-stage (III–IV) diagnosis using multivariable logistic regression, interaction tests, and sensitivity analyses (drug-type disaggregation, alternative stage definitions, missing-stage sensitivity). Expected outcome: Provide evidence on whether recent-onset analgesic prescribing or anxiety/depression recordings are associated with increased odds of advanced-stage diagnosis and whether persistent conditions are associated with reduced odds, informing hypotheses about surveillance versus alternative-explanation mechanisms and prioritization of diagnostic investigation. Experiments: Datasets: Linked England National Cancer Registry (incident lung C34 and colon C18 diagnoses 2012–2018) + CPRD primary care records (consultations, Readcodes, prescription Prodcodes, haemoglobin) with area-level deprivation and patient demographics. Inclusion: patients with ≥1 GP record in 12 months pre-diagnosis, registered at UpToStandard practice for ≥12 months. Exposures: chronic analgesic medication use and anxiety/depression categorized as Not Present, Recent-onset (<12 months pre-diagnosis only), Historic (12–72 months only), Persistent (records in both windows). Additional exposure disaggregation: opioid vs non-opioid analgesic prescriptions; anxiety and depression modeled separately. Outcome: cancer stage dichotomized primary analysis as Early (I–II) vs Advanced (III–IV); sensitivity analysis Early (I–III) vs Advanced (IV). Baselines: (1) unadjusted model; (2) multivariable logistic regression with binary comorbidity flags; (3) model using Charlson index or Cambridge Multimorbidity Score; (4) model using prescription counts only. Primary model: multivariable logistic regression adjusted for age (categorical), sex, IMD income quintile, number of GP consultations (30 days excluded), number of physical comorbidities, site-specific and general cancer symptoms, haemoglobin-confirmed anaemia. Evaluation metrics: adjusted odds ratios (aOR) with 95% CI and p-values for exposures; model discrimination (c-statistic/AUC) and calibration (Hosmer-Lemeshow or calibration plot), AIC, Brier score. Statistical tests: interaction terms (exposure × age, exposure × sex), likelihood-ratio tests for interaction significance, Wald tests for exposure contrasts. Ablation studies: (A) remove consultation frequency covariate to assess mediation by healthcare utilization; (B) replace duration exposure with binary ever/never to quantify loss of effect information; (C) restrict to opioid-only prescriptions vs non-opioid; (D) separate anxiety and depression as independent exposures. Sensitivity analyses: multiple look-back windows (24, 36, 72 months), alternative missing-stage handling (complete-case vs multiple imputation), redefinition of consultations window (exclude 90 days), and subgroup analyses by age bands and sex. Reported outputs: aORs for each exposure category, interaction p-values, change in AUC and AIC across models, and results of ablation contrasts with corresponding 95% CIs. Risk Factors and Limitations: Missing or misclassified data: stage missingness (~10–15%) causes selection bias; mental-health conditions are under-recorded leading to exposure misclassification. Reverse causality: analgesic escalation may reflect undiagnosed cancer symptoms (confounding by indication). Residual confounding: unmeasured socio-behavioral variables, symptom severity, or healthcare-seeking behavior may bias associations. Measurement error: prescription records do not guarantee consumption; inability to precisely time symptom onset vs recording. Generalizability: results derived from English primary care and registry data may not transfer to other health systems. Model limitations: logistic regression estimates associations not causal effects; interactions and stratified estimates may be unstable in small subgroups. Scalability and compute: linked dataset size requires secure data environment but poses modest compute demands; complex imputation or causal inference methods may require additional resources. Interpretability limits: observed associations cannot definitively distinguish surveillance vs alternative-explanation mechanisms without additional longitudinal or qualitative evidence.
